summary: Isles of Shoals Light on White Island, New Hampshire: a light since 1820-21, a keeper's household whose daughter became the poet Celia Thaxter, automated in 1986 and state-owned.

lens.note: Second-order Fresnel lens (USLHS); removed for a modern beacon a few years after automation (LighthouseFriends). Current optic is a solar LED unit.

structures.note: 58 ft from base to lantern centre (USLHS). Stone base of the first tower retained (LighthouseFriends).
First tower. Height disputed: 40 ft tower (LighthouseFriends) or 87 ft (Putnam).

access.note: Owned by the State of New Hampshire. Grounds open, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The archive lists it as not open to the public (USLHS).

visit.note: Cruises that pass the light run from the mainland (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: State of New Hampshire (Division of Parks and Recreation)

events.note: Act approved 1 May 1820 authorizes a light on one of the Isles of Shoals (the act title).
USLHS "Year Established: 1821". LighthouseFriends dates the first rubblestone lighthouse to 1820.
Rubble-stone tower, 1821 (Putnam). Height disputed: LighthouseFriends 40 ft tower; Putnam 87 ft.
Thomas B. Laighton principal keeper (USLHS roster; LighthouseFriends gives $600 salary and the same year in its account).
New lantern and apparatus by Winslow Lewis at $3,600 (LighthouseFriends).
L. H. D. Shepherd principal keeper after Laighton resigned (USLHS roster; LighthouseFriends).
Second-order Fresnel lens (USLHS). LighthouseFriends places a second-order lens in the 1859 tower.
Cylindrical brick tower replaces the stone tower (USLHS; LighthouseFriends). Thaxter, writing in 1873, dates the change to about ten years earlier.
Board report of 1875 calls the old stone dwelling scarcely habitable (LighthouseFriends quoting the report).
Wood-framed one-and-a-half story duplex, completed two years after the 1875 report (LighthouseFriends).
Mineral oil replaces lard oil as the illuminant (LighthouseFriends).
Brick oil house built (Board report for fiscal year ended 30 June 1892).
Board report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1896 (scan p. 53): the fog signal on White Island is a bell.
Automated fog bell; a first-class air siren placed later (LighthouseFriends).
USLHS "Year Automated: 1986". Coast Guard personnel removed after a three-month automation process (LighthouseFriends). Wikipedia-type sources give 1987; not used.
White Island and some other islands transferred to New Hampshire State Parks (LighthouseFriends).
April 2003: $250,000 Save America's Treasures grant (LighthouseFriends).
Tower repaired and given stucco; dwelling reroofed (LighthouseFriends).
Storm of 19 April 2007 destroys the covered walkway, foghorn and solar panels (LighthouseFriends; USLHS).
Covered walkway reconstructed (USLHS "reconstructed in 2011").

keepers.name: Eliza Laighton
keepers.note: Wife of Thomas B. Laighton. LighthouseFriends says the wife, children and a hired hand did most of the keeping; SeacoastHistory names her Eliza. Not on the USLHS roster.

keepers.name: Celia Thaxter
keepers.note: Laighton daughter. As a girl she was allowed to light the lamps (her own account); not a roster keeper and no years given.

keepers.name: John Downs
keepers.note: Acting keeper while the head keeper went ashore, in an undated March gale (LighthouseFriends). Not on the USLHS roster.

wrecks.outcome: An islander remembered the wreck in Thaxter's account, with beaches strewn with almond-nuts for years afterwards. The place of the wreck is not given beyond the Shoals.
Brig, homeward bound from Spain. Thaxter says the vessel and all her crew were lost, seen from the island during a storm.
Grounded near the tower in a March gale; the acting keeper John Downs and a friend, with the keeper, rescued the crew using a line (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata gives 1790 (built) and 1865 (first_lit). The USLHS record (established 1821; brick tower 1859) and LighthouseFriends (rubblestone first light 1820; brick tower 1859) do not support those dates. The 1820 act authorized the first light, so no 1790 tower is supported by the sources read.
The 1859 brick tower date is given by both the archive and LighthouseFriends; the record's 1865 date has no independent support among the sources read.

The 'is a bell' statement is the Board report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1896 (scan 53). The renewed recommendation at scan 295 is in the report for 1897, so the earlier citation was wrong. The 1901 report keeps the White Island recommendation as a past one and now recommends Boon Island.

Not resolved. SeacoastHistory says he left for the island 'never to return'; LighthouseFriends says he vowed never to set foot on the mainland again and went on attending to business there. The story states the disagreement.

corrections.why: The brick tower now standing was built in 1859 (USLHS; LighthouseFriends). The record's 1790 appears only as a Wikidata inception date with no supporting account of a tower then.
The 1865 first_lit (Wikidata) is not supported by the archive (established 1821) or LighthouseFriends (rubblestone first light, 1820).
The archive gives 58 ft from base to the centre of the lantern (about 17.7 m).

notes_for_editor:
Keeper roster: 166 USLHS lines matched to the station by name and position (0.06 km). Lines are the archive's own (NARA registers via Kraig Anderson); not checked against primary registers. Three non-keeper stints (contractors, blacksmith, foreman) and 47 USCG-heading lines are kept as role "other" with the archive heading in note.
Conflicts left open: (1) first light 1820 (LighthouseFriends) vs 1821 (USLHS, Putnam); (2) heights: LighthouseFriends 40 ft tower plus about 10 ft lantern; Putnam and Hawthorne 87 ft (Putnam calls it the tower, Hawthorne the lantern); (3) brick tower year: 1859 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends) vs about 1863 (Thaxter, counted back from 1873); (4) second-order lens 1855 (USLHS) vs 1859 tower (LighthouseFriends); (5) automation 1986 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends) vs 1987 in a Wikipedia lead and Cyberlights (not cited); (6) Lighthouse Kids funding; (7) the 2007 storm: LighthouseFriends says 19 April 2007.
Brick vs granite: a Wikipedia lead and Cyberlights say granite walls; the archive says brick. Not resolved (Coast Guard historian page is blocked; the Internet Archive capture returned only its index). Left out of the story.
Coast Guard historian page (history.uscg.mil Isle of Shoals Light) returned 403 for the live site and only a capture index from web.archive.org; the article text was not read. The Coast Guard PDF (media.defense.gov LHNH.PDF) returned 403. Both would settle the tower date.
Pocahontas 1839: only Thaxter's memoir (written 1873). New Hampshire Gazette 1839-40 search (Chronicling America) returned only ship arrivals and an excursion notice under the name Pocahontas; the wreck is not confirmed by a newspaper. Keep the attribution to Thaxter.
Sagunto 1813: Thaxter records an islander's memory of the wreck; the account does not place it at the light. The link between the 1813 loss and the 1820 act is claimed by secondary sites and is not established by any source read; the story does not make it.
Russian brig (LighthouseFriends): undated, no newspaper check made.
Laighton: a NH Historical Society catalogue entry, seen only in a search snippet (not read), gives "Laighton, Henry B. (-1865)", Keeper of White Island Lighthouse. SeacoastHistory gives Thomas B. Laighton (1804-1866). Not used; the forename and death year disagree and should be checked. LighthouseFriends' keeper list also gives "Laighton" for 1839-41 and 1843-49, matching the archive.
Thaxter says the family lived in the cottage "for six years"; the roster shows Laighton off the island between 1841 and 1843 (Joseph Cheever keeper). Not reconciled.
Hawthorne: quoted from the SeacoastNH transcription of Passages from the American Note-Books (1868); the book itself was not read. Gossip about the keeper's wives and drinking in the same entry is not used.
Access: USLHS says "Open to Public: No"; LighthouseFriends says grounds open, dwelling and tower closed. Both are reported in the story.
Record fields not verified: characteristic (Fl W 15s, both in the record and Wikipedia) is not checked against the Light List and is not in facts. Fog horn in the record vs fog bell and air siren (LighthouseFriends).
The Bulletin for 1913 (PDF p. 12) lists "Isles of Shoals, N. Y." among illuminant changes: probably a state error for N.H. Not used.
No photos mirrored: LighthouseFriends photographs are copyrighted.
Budget: six websearch.py queries were run for this station (the guide allows three); the extra ones were for the Sagunto wreck, the Coast Guard historian page and the Thaxter text. Not WebSearch. Keeper detail from the Official Register was not checked.
Printed page numbers are not read: all Internet Archive citations use scan page numbers. Check the page images before printing a page number.
Verification 2026-10-27 corrections: (a) the 1896 'is a bell' citation was scan 295, which lies in the report for 1897 (its text says 'made in the Board's last annual report, is renewed'); the FY1896 statement is at scan 53, now cited. (b) The 1901 report's Boon Island conclusion was omitted; it is now stated. (c) 'About seven miles (11 km)' had no source in the footnotes; replaced by LighthouseFriends' 'six miles' for the group. (d) 'best-documented keeper' was unsourced and removed. (e) 'Spanish ship' for the Sagunto is not in Thaxter's text and was removed from the wreck entry. (f) Thaxter's 'another storm' for the covered-walk loss is not in her text: she describes a southeast storm that carried the walk away (undated) and a southeast storm that broke the windows; the story no longer says they are different storms. (g) Celia's age: Thaxter says 'scarcely five years old'; SeacoastHistory gives four. The story gives both. (h) Laighton's residence: SeacoastHistory ('never to return') and LighthouseFriends (the vow, business on the mainland) disagree; the story states it. (i) Putnam (1917) is a general history in the corpus; it is cited here for a station fact (the first tower's height and light) only as a disagreement with LighthouseFriends and USLHS, which the editor should accept or drop. (j) Hawthorne is quoted from the SeacoastNH transcription (checked: the 'eighty-seven feet' and 'peeling his harvest of onions' sentences are there). (k) The Board page checks: 1892 entry scan 380 (FY1892, after its header); 1901 scan 73 (printed 51); 1820 Act scan 62; Putnam scan 102-103.
